schools.summary: Gregory the Great reads the scene as the adversary's last device: having failed by the loss of substance and children and by the goading of the wife, the enemy brings in the friends to overcome with bitter words the man whom scourges could not subdue.
Gill marks Bildad's harsher second turn: no counsel now, only heaped charges painting the wicked man's misery as near to Job's as he can, to prove the greatly afflicted Job wicked.
Henry hears Bildad shoot bitter words, serving Satan's design, and gathers the opening charges: idle talk, regardlessness, disdain, outrageous passion, and giving law to Providence.
Clarke reads passionate invective (Heath's analysis): downright abuse meant to terrify Job into compliance by a dreadful picture of the wicked man's end.
Ellicott notes only that Bildad begins very much as Job himself had done at the head of chapter 16.

themes: a wise tongue bent to the tempter's purpose

schools.summary: Gill reads the plural as addressed to more than one, chiding the friends for letting the dispute be drawn out with a hardened man when it is high time to have done.

Clarke labours the Chaldee philology (Good's 'thorns,' Schultens's 'snares') and takes the plural of all present; Wesley reads it as Eastern idiom for Job alone, 'mark' meaning consider the matter better.
Keil and Delitzsch render 'how long will ye hunt for words?', conceding that from the root for 'end' the word yields no clear sense unless 'close upon close, beginning anew.'

debates.question: How should the disputed Hebrew word (qintsey) be rendered?

sides.position: 'make an end of words' — from the root for end or limit
'hunt for words,' or 'thorns / snares set among words' — from an Arabic or Chaldee root

themes: how long ere ye make an end of words

schools.summary: Gill traces the grievance to Job's sending them to the beasts (ch. 12) and slighting their wisdom (ch. 17), and turns it back: man is brutish before God, but self-sufficient men resent having their understanding questioned ('are we blind also?').
Clarke: 'thou treatest us as if we had neither reason nor understanding'; Wesley glosses 'beasts' as ignorant, stupid men (ch. 17).

Ellicott traces the reference to Job's contempt (chs. 13, 16), marks the rising harshness, and notes the chapter works out a single simile like ch. 8, the two similes touching at v.16; the plural is used as of one representing a class.

themes: wherefore are we counted as beasts

schools.summary: Gill: the Hebrew is 'his soul' — Bildad throws Job's own word back, making him a madman tearing his own flesh and soul, a charge of impatience ill-suiting Job.
Clarke: 'thou eatest thy own flesh'; must God work a miracle to exempt thee from the common lot? Wesley: shall God's counsels, firmer than rocks, be altered to thy humours?
Ellicott exposes the closing clause as lifted from Job's own words (ch. 14) and turned to Bildad's purpose — a wilful perversion.

Henry draws the lesson: whatever befalls is by God's counsel, word, and settled providence — absurd to think the earth forsaken or the rock removed for one man, though the rebuke, truly aimed, would stand.

outliers.note: Identifies the closing clause about the rock as a direct quotation from Job in chapter 14, wilfully perverted by Bildad to a sense opposite to Job's own.

themes: he teareth himself in his anger
shall the earth be forsaken for thee

schools.summary: Gill reads 'yea' as 'nevertheless' and takes the quenched light as the moral light of nature and conscience, justly taken from an abuser (Cocceius: the light of doctrine).
Clarke would read an imprecation — 'let the light of the wicked be extinguished' — the abused understanding taken away; from here to the chapter's end all is invective.
Keil and Delitzsch keep the tent-lamp figure ('fate has put out my lamp') and note that 'spark' (shabib, only here in Hebrew) is read variously as spark, flame, or brightness.

Henry: the wicked man's light is a spark and a candle, not the light of the Lord (Isa. 50:11), put out with him at death when his expectation perishes (Prov. 11:7); yet the application to Job is unjust.

debates.question: What is the 'light' that is put out?

sides.position: the inward light of nature, reason, and conscience
the outward light of prosperity and of a man's house

themes: the light of the wicked put out
the spark that shall not shine

schools.summary: Gill: not the eye's light but reason ('if the light in a man be darkness, how great is that darkness'), and best of all the light of prosperity in house and family, now obscured.
Clarke reads outward ruin — property pillaged, family untimely end; the candle put out with him meaning no posterity, lamp and line extinguished together.
Keil and Delitzsch keep the hanging tent-lamp of ch. 29 and the fourfold quenched-light figure, and carry the picture into the straitened steps (contrast Prov. 4:12).

themes: the light dark in his tabernacle
the candle put out with him

schools.summary: Gill contrasts the strong strides of health and prosperity with the hedged, thorn-blocked steps of adversity, where no way of escape can be found.
Clarke: the dupe and victim of his own airy, impious schemes; Wesley reads 'the steps of his strength' as his strong enterprises now hindered and entangled.
Ellicott renders 'his giant strides' and presses the irony: his own devices, when they promise prosperity, lead him to destruction.

outliers.note: Opens the reading that governs vv.7-13 — the language is drawn throughout from the arts of the hunt, the quarry driven from a broad base into ever-narrowing ground.

themes: the steps of his strength straitened
his own counsel casts him down

schools.summary: Gill: 'by his own feet' — the man walks into the net himself; the pit he digs he falls into, and his own sins are the snares that entice and hold him.
Clarke: like a wild beast taken in a net, the more he flounces to free himself the more he is entangled, forever walking on the meshes.
Ellicott sets it against Job's 'hunted by the Almighty' (ch. 10), insinuates Job's self-caused calamity, and notes the deliberate heaping of every word for the art of snaring.

themes: cast into a net by his own feet

schools.summary: Gill: the gin holds him fast; God has snares and gins in plenty, is said to rain them down, and is himself a snare, so that there is no escaping his hands.
Henry names 'the robber' as Satan, a murderer and robber from the beginning, who lays snares in every path and hunts for the precious life.
Keil and Delitzsch trace the step-by-step march to total destruction, every clause a curse being fulfilled, the gin seizing the heel and the noose drawing tight.
Clarke notes Houbigant's reorder of vv.9-10 and unfolds the whole hunt of vv.7-13 — the exhausted quarry fallen on by the huntsman.

debates.question: Who is 'the robber' that prevails against him?

sides.position: Satan the tempter, a robber and murderer from the beginning
the huntsman falling on the exhausted quarry (the figure kept within the hunt)

themes: the gin takes him by the heel

schools.summary: Gill: the snare is hidden in the ground, for in vain is the net spread in the sight of any bird (Prov. 1:17); the cord that springs it is kept hidden in the fowler's hand.
Keil and Delitzsch set the two clauses parallel — snare hidden in the earth, nets upon the path — so that neither standing still nor walking on is safe.
Clarke folds the verse into the hunt: pitfalls and gins set within the narrowing ground, so that many are taken before the lines of beaters close.

themes: the snare laid in the ground

schools.summary: Gill makes the man a 'Magor-missabib' (Jer. 20) and multiplies the terrors — of earthly judges, of a guilty conscience, of the broken law, of God's judgments, and of death.
Ellicott compares ch. 15:21 and reads the verb as 'chase him at his heels' rather than the tempting 'startle him to his feet.'

Henry: the terrors of conscience haunt him on every side — heaven frowning, hell gaping, earth sick of him — driving him to flee like the guilty who run when none pursue (Prov. 28:1), though his feet are fast in the snare.

themes: the way of sin is a way of fear

schools.summary: Gill reads 'his strength' first as famine-struck vigour, then records the Jewish reading of 'his strength' as his children (Reuben, Gen. 49; Targum: his firstborn son; Jarchi: his son; Ben Gersom: his seed).
Clarke keeps the exhausted-quarry figure and cites the Chaldee — 'let his firstborn son be famished, and affliction prepared for his wife.'
Ellicott keeps the literal sense of bodily strength but notes the firstborn-son option, and reads 'destruction ready' as ready 'for his halting,' waiting for his tripping.
Henry: what the sinner relied on — wealth, power, friends, his own spirit — fails him, hunger-bitten, while destruction stands ready to seize him in a moment (Ps. 73:19).

debates.question: Does 'his strength' mean the man's own vigour, or his children?

sides.position: his own bodily strength and resources, worn out when the blow falls
his children — the firstborn son, the strength of his house, cut off by famine

schools.summary: Gill offers 'the bars' or 'branches of his skin' (the veins), famine wasting the man to a skeleton, and records the Jewish reading that takes the 'branches' for his children.

Keil and Delitzsch read the 'bars' as the body's members and 'the firstborn of death' (cf. Isa. 14:30) as the deadliest disease; Ellicott renders 'the members of his body,' the firstborn of death a wasting disease like Job's.
Clarke reads a sudden, overwhelming mortal stroke (Chaldee: the angel of death consume his children); Wesley: simply a terrible kind of death, the firstborn eminent in its kind.
Henry: arrested by the firstborn of death — a disease or stroke of uncommon strength, 'so great a death' (2 Cor. 1:10) — that devours the strength of his skin and brings rottenness to his bones.

sides.position: a wasting disease — death's eldest and deadliest child
simply death in its most terrible form, the eminent kind

themes: devouring the strength of his skin

schools.summary: Gill turns over 'his confidence' (wealth, children, health, or hope of heaven) and offers the reversed reading — rooted out of the tabernacle that was his confidence, the soul plucked from the body.

Wesley takes 'king of terrors' flatly for death (Aristotle's 'most terrible of terribles'); Clarke doubts the phrase is warranted, preferring 'as a king / destroyer,' Good's 'dissolution shall invade him as a monarch,' with Dr. Stock's caution.
Ellicott exalts 'the king of terrors' as perhaps the most remarkable personification of unseen forces in the Bible, and reads 'rooted out of his tent which he trusted was his own.'
Henry preaches death as the king of terrors — terrible to nature (John 12:27), doubly so to the wicked, but by Christ so disarmed as to become the saints' friend and servant.

debates.question: Is 'the king of terrors' a warranted figure of death, or a doubtful reading?

sides.position: death personified — a vivid and remarkable figure
the beautiful phrase is not warranted by the Hebrew — read 'as a king' or 'as a destroyer'

themes: death personified or a doubtful reading

schools.summary: Gill owns that the subject 'it' is left blank in the text, the conjectures many.

Clarke personifies Desolation as the new inhabitant (with a Persian couplet) and offers brimstone as either Sodom or an ancient purifying custom, though most likely Bildad glances at Job's own ruin (ch. 1); Wesley makes the dweller Destruction, the house doomed as unjustly got, the brimstone recalling Sodom.
Ellicott reads 'they that are none of his' — strangers in a tent no longer his — and takes the brimstone for the cities of the plain (Gen. 19).
Henry: the house shares the owner's curse, unjustly got and so neither comfortable nor lasting, death itself taking possession.

sides.position: strangers — 'they that are none of his'

themes: it shall dwell in his tabernacle

schools.summary: Gill reads the dried roots as the extinct family, or the exhausted substance, like Ephraim smitten and his root dried up.
Clarke: total ruin — self, posterity, and property, as a tree whose every branch is lopped and every root cut away.
Ellicott hears the deliberate echo of Bildad's earlier plant (ch. 8) and of Job's already-slain children.
Henry: the fate of houses rooted only in earth (Jeroboam, Baasha, Ahab); but those rooted in Christ do not wither, and the threatening image becomes an invitation.

themes: rooted in earth or in Christ

schools.summary: Gill: forgotten of God and of men, the very monuments built to keep his memory perishing with him.
Keil and Delitzsch take up the run of clauses to the chapter's end and gloss 'his day' as the day of doom; Ellicott notes the dread of a lost name among the desert-roamers (cf. Jer. 35:19).
Clarke: none to continue his name, never a man of reputation, none to talk of his fame after his death.
Henry sets the antithesis — his name never written in heaven (Luke 10:20); the memory of the just is blessed, but the name of the wicked shall rot (Prov. 10:7).

themes: the name of the wicked shall rot

schools.summary: Gill traces the light-to-darkness senses and lingers on the plural 'they shall drive him' — God, or the angels good and bad, hurrying him into endless night.
Clarke reads a violent death, the man dragged away reluctant in his iniquity; Wesley: from a prosperous life to disgrace and the grave, the land of darkness.
Keil and Delitzsch set the clause in the march of doom, the man chased out of the world as one hunted from the society of the living.
Henry: chased as Adam from paradise, thrust from a world weary of him into the darkness of the grave and the outer darkness beyond (Ps. 49:19).
Gill reads 'nephew' as a son's son (Targum, Jarchi, Bar Tzemach) and catches Bildad's error — Job had afterward as many children as before.
Clarke gives Coverdale's fuller version, in which young and old are astonished at the man's death.
Ellicott renders 'neither his own son's son among his people, nor any remaining where he sojourned'; Keil and Delitzsch keep the double negation, the household swept clean.
Henry grants sin's curse on posterity but denies the inference — the childless are not thereby graceless, there being a better name than sons and daughters (Isa. 56:5).
Gill takes 'they that come after' temporally — younger survivors or later posterity, thunderstruck at the sudden ruin.
Clarke and Wesley read the terms temporally — the young astonished at the report, the aged contemporaries who saw the judgment seized with horror (achazu saar).

Ellicott glosses 'his day' as his doom, the man a monument to all who come after; Keil and Delitzsch take the two words geographically — those who dwell in the west and in the east, the whole world aghast.
Henry dwells on the awe — so sudden and dreadful the fall that all cry, 'how terrible art thou in thy judgments!' (cf. Deut. 28:37).

debates.question: Are 'they that come after' and 'they that went before' marks of time or of place?

sides.position: time — later generations and older contemporaries
place — those who dwell in the west and those in the east

themes: the fall made a public horror

schools.summary: Gill gathers the whole picture into the verdict and notes the Targum makes the line the very cry of the astonished onlookers.
Keil and Delitzsch render the couplet as the formal seal of the discourse; Ellicott presses the singular 'him that knoweth not God' as designedly aimed at Job.
Clarke reads it as the common lot of the wicked, plainly meant for Job — 'Poor Job! hard was thy lot, severe were thy sufferings.'
Henry takes it for the chapter's theology — the beginning is a wilful ignorance of God, the end utter destruction (2 Thess. 1:8).

outliers.note: Holds that Bildad's deliberate use of the singular 'the place of him that knoweth not God' shows he designedly meant the whole terrible and cruel picture to represent Job himself.

themes: such are the dwellings of the wicked
the place of him that knows not God
